If you wanted to know all the jobs that AI will produce, look no further than cybersecurity. This is going to become one of the biggest investment areas for enterprises going forward. 

And even as the work becomes more agentic and autonomous you will need more talent to point the agents at the most critical work, review findings, patch systems, respond to incidents, and more. 

Lots of opportunity right now for the systems that protect data and enterprises, as well as the professionals that are deploying them and protecting organizations.

It’s going to only get more wild out there.

Any form of security through obscurity is fully over. This barely worked as a method with humans, but just simply is over in a world of autonomous systems that will look through every crevice and try every permutation of attack possible.

As a result, years and years of legacy enterprise infrastructure will need to be upgraded, security practices modernized, data pipelines cleaned up, access controls better managed, and much more. Agents will help on the defensive side because they can both accelerate this work and equally simulate the risk vectors.

But there’s a long road ahead to prepare for this future. This is also partially why diffusion timelines will take longer than some realize.

Agent swarms for cyber defense is about to be one of the biggest categories in AI. We are going to have agents reviewing our code and infra, testing every permutation of risk, processing gobs of data, and more. 

Security is one of the best use-cases for swarms because it’s an obvious area where more compute in equals more value out. There’s a wide range of testing that people can never get around to - or at least quickly enough - that agents have no problem going after. 

Going to be a wild time in cyber.

Kimi K3.1 Pro launches at 4th on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index scoring 55, making large gains in agentic performance; it will be the leading open-weights model once its weights are published

@Kimi_Moonshot's new reasoning model gains 11 points over Kimi K3 (max, 44). It trails only Claude Opus 5.5 (max with fallback, 58), Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max with fallback, 56), and Muse Wonder Full (max, 56) on the Intelligence Index.

Once the weights for K3.1 Pro are released it will be the highest-scoring open weights model and the gap between the leading open weights and proprietary models on the Intelligence Index will narrow from 12 points to 3.

Key results:
➤ Large gains in agentic performance: Kimi K3.1 Pro scores 3rd on GDPval-AA with 1,846 Elo, up 312 Elo from Kimi K3, behind only Claude Opus 5.5 (1,866 Elo) and Muse Wonder Full (1,857 Elo). Kimi K3.1 Pro also achieves the highest score of any model on Terminal-Bench 4.0. K3.1 Pro scores 67%, up from 13% for Kimi K3 and ahead of Claude Sonnet 5.5 (64%). AutomationBench-AA, which tests agentic SaaS workflows, rises from 58% to 73%.

➤ Gains in other evals are more moderate: Humanity's Last Exam rises from 47% to 52%, CritPt from 23% to 25%, and SciCode from 59% to 61%. AA-Omniscience Index rises from 20 to 30, as the hallucination rate falls from 53% to 44% and accuracy rises from 48% to 51%.

➤ Cost per Task roughly equal to Kimi K3 at $1.98 per Task: K3.1 Pro uses 55K output tokens per Intelligence Index task, 14% more than Kimi K3 at 48K, while its first-party token prices are 33% lower.

Additional model details:
➤ Context window: 1M tokens.
➤ Size: 2.8T total, 104B active parameters
➤ Input modalities: Text and image
➤ Weights and license: Weights currently not published, Moonshot is expected to release the weights soon after launch
➤ Pricing: $2/$10/$0.20 per 1M input/output/cache hit tokens, 33% lower than Kimi K3 on all three rates.

Congratulations to the team at @Kimi_Moonshot on the release!

Announcing Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index v2.0: FrontierCode v1.1 from Cognition replaces DeepSWE, SWE-Atlas-QnA grading is revised, and Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code leads at 61.7

Today we are launching v2.0 of the Coding Agent Index. The Index evaluates models together with their agent harnesses, now across 290 tasks covering software engineering, terminal use, and repository Q&A, with the three benchmarks weighted equally.

Changelog (Index v1.5 → Index v2.0):

→ FrontierCode v1.1 replaces DeepSWE v1.1. FrontierCode is a benchmark from @cognition with a private test set: 100 software engineering tasks on real open-source repositories, graded on whether a maintainer would merge the change. An attempt that fails a blocking check scores zero, and one that passes them all scores between 70% and 100% depending on the non-blocking checks it meets. We also scan each trajectory with a modified version of Cognition's rule-based scanner, and any attempt flagged for accessing solution material scores zero.

→ Revised SWE-Atlas-QnA grading, now SWE-Atlas-QnA-AA. Scale AI's 124 repository Q&A tasks are unchanged. We reworded 127 of the 1,306 rubric criteria for more consistent verdicts and moved to GPT-6 Luna (xhigh) as the judge, with five votes per criterion. The dataset and judge configuration are published on Hugging Face.

Key results:

➤ Claude Opus 5.5 leads the Index: Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5 (max) scores 61.7, followed by Claude Code with Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max) at 59.3, Muse Code with Muse Wonder Full (max) at 58.9 and Claude Code with Claude Fable 5.1 (max with fallback) at 57.6.

➤ FrontierCode v1.1 is where Opus 5.5 pulls ahead: Opus 5.5 scores 56.0% on FrontierCode, ahead of Codex with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (max) at 52.6%, Codex with GPT-6.1 Sol (max) at 49.4% and Codex with GPT-6 Astra (max) at 49.3%. Below the top, FrontierCode scores are tightly packed: 15 of the 24 configurations on the Index score between 43% and 49%.

➤ SWE-Atlas-QnA-AA grading is stricter and more consistent: across the 21 configurations evaluated on both Index versions, the mean score falls 1.7 points, from 58.8% to 57.1%, with 14 of 21 moving down. Individual configurations move by up to 7 points: Muse Code with Muse Spark Open (xhigh) falls 7.0, Kimi K3 in Kimi Code CLI and Codex with GPT-6 Luna (max) 6.2, and Muse Code with Muse Wonder (max) 5.6, while Codex with GPT-6.1 Sol (max) gains 2.1.

➤ Four configurations sit on the cost frontier: Codex with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (max) scores 47.3 at $0.39 per task, Codex with GPT-6.1 Sol (max) 54.1 at $1.50, Codex with GPT-6 Astra (max) 54.7 at $7.04 and Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5 (max) 61.7 at $11.42. Costs are pay-per-token API costs, not subscription prices.

We will keep updating the Coding Agent Index incrementally, with more evaluations and agents to come.

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 is the new #1 openly-available model in the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index. Other proprietary models may offer better cyber defense performance but are restricted access

@deepseek_ai recently released DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, an update to their flagship open-weights model DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. With an Artificial Analysis Cyber Index score of 57%, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 is the #1 openly-available model for cyber defense capabilities.

The Artificial Analysis Cyber Index measures capability on agentic cyber defense tasks and is composed of three benchmarks: CWE-Bench-AA, DeepsecBench-AA and CyberGym-E2E-AA. The Cyber Index primarily evaluates models through their publicly accessible APIs, reflecting the cyber capabilities available to developers.

Many models, particularly proprietary models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google, may have stronger defensive cyber capabilities but encounter safety refusals that reduce their overall scores. GPT-6 Sol (Daybreak Blue, max), available through OpenAI’s trusted-access program, leads the Index, scoring 32 points above its public counterpart driven by fewer refusals. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 encounters no safety refusals.

Key results:

➤ DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 has the highest score among publicly-available models on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index and #2 position overall. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (max) scores 57% ahead of the previously leading publicly-available models Grok 4.7 (xhigh) and MiMo-V2.6-Pro by 1 point. It places #2 overall, with the trusted-access model GPT-6 Sol (Daybreak Blue, max) leading by 12 points with a score of 69%

➤ DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 improves on its predecessor DeepSeek V4.1 Flash by 16 points. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (max)’s 16-point improvement from 41% to 57% is driven by a substantial 53-point improvement on CyberGym-E2E-AA from 23% to 76%. On CWE-Bench-AA and DeepsecBench-AA it scores 69% and 25%, compared to 68% and 31% for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (max)

➤ With a Cost per Task of $0.42, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 sits on the Capability vs. Cost Pareto frontier. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 costs $0.42 per task, more than 2x MiMo-V2.6-Pro (56%) at $0.18 per task but 4x cheaper than GPT-6 Sol (Daybreak Blue, max, 69%) at $1.77 per task

tweets.text: This seems right to me, unfortunately, and it is essentially a species of interest-rate rise (the opportunity cost of capital is increasing). It is true that forward and futures markets for compute, and making compute into a financial commodity, would help here.

I am also optimistic that AI/cyber will be defense-friendly after things stabilize, but before that it will be offense-friendly, which creates a lot of dynamics that are difficult to model:

1. For any existing or new vulnerabilities discovered by governments and other offensive actors, there will be an incentive to exploit them quickly, rather than sit on them quietly, because they will anticipate that the defender will find the vulnerability and patch it much faster than before.
2. The surface area of cyber is very broad, and finding vulnerabilities is different from fixing them, which is also different from fixing them without also introducing new, even subtler security problems into the code. 
3. We do not know how high the ceiling for subtle bugs might be. Do there exist vulnerabilities that were simply too hard for humans to find or laborious to exploit? How many vulnerabilities? How long will they persist? We are now getting to the point where we have to reason about systems with quasi-superhuman cognitive performance. This is hard! Counter-intuitive things will happen.
4. There are some threats such as hardware vulnerabilities or new discoveries in cryptography where the offense/defense dynamics could be importantly different from traditional cyber. 

There was always going to be some tumult as models gained cyber capabilities. This was by far the easiest major novel AI risk to project, in broad terms. It may be true that broad and rapid diffusion is the optimal path forward; that outcome wouldn’t surprise me that much. But it could also be true that, given the offense-favoring dynamics at first and the uncertainties I have described, it’ll be optimal to slow diffusion. And regardless of whether it is optimal to do so, I would expect substantial political pressure to “do something” if the cyber events are sufficiently damaging or disruptive. 

The optimal outcome is one where we diffuse fast and comprehensively enough to find and fix vulnerabilities while also not causing too much tumult. Maybe we are striking the balance effectively now, as a global industry! I hope so. But I also hope everyone is attentive and ready to update their beliefs/strategies as we gather empirical data. I’m skeptical of anyone who seems confident here in either direction. 

Near as I can tell, despite a lot of scary potential, nothing truly catastrophic has happened yet (the water is running; the lights are on, no cataclysmic data breaches I am aware of). I hope that continues to be the case. I do agree with the AI risk skeptics that there is a lot of catastrophizing on X about this, and the current attacks, while significant, seem well within the range of things we can bounce back from. 

If things continue at this level of severity, I feel pretty good about our situation with AI/cyber. But if it gets noticeably worse and seems to be on a trend of getting even more severe, which is my expectation, we could be in for trouble. Maybe society can digest way more cyberattacks than I had apprehended. Maybe “cybersecurity is not very important” as the famous saying/paper goes. I’m very much open to being pleasantly surprised.

be very careful if you find yourself simply passing messages to and from your agents

e.g. people ask you a question on slack, and you simply ask an agent and pass its response back - it should be obvious that your job can be automated in that case

instead, you should try and build an agent (or sometimes just skills) that can reliably answer similar questions moving forward and remove yourself from the loop

your value then becomes improving said agents and skills, and your impact can easily scale and manifest even when you sleep

don’t be automated. be the automator
